extracted.intended_audience: psychologists and researchers conducting measurement development/validation for humor-related temperament (STCI) and users of the STCI in research or applied settings
extracted.subtask_description: Adapting the State-Trait Cheerfulness Inventory (long and short forms) into English and validating its psychometric properties (factorial, convergent/discriminant, predictive validity, reliability, sensitivity) across self- and peer-report samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three core traits (construct definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The instrument assesses three temperamentally based dimensions relevant to sense of humor: cheerfulness (low threshold for amusement), seriousness (cognitive frame that raises threshold for amusement), and bad mood (affective states that raise threshold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cheerfulness lowers the threshold for amusement and predisposes to smiling/laughter and humor behavior. Seriousness and bad mood heighten the threshold for amusement for different reasons (cognitive vs affective). The three traits are treated as distinct but correlated higher-order factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facet structure for each trait
rubrics_metrics.description: Trait cheerfulness, seriousness and bad mood are each composed of inter-correlated facets (CH: five facets; SE: six facets; BM: five facets) that together form the higher-order trait scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cheerfulness facets: CH1 prevalence of cheerful mood, CH2 low threshold for smiling and laughter, CH3 composed view of adverse circumstances, CH4 broad range of active elicitors, CH5 cheerful interaction style. Bad mood facets include predominance of bad mood, sadness, ill-humoredness and behaviors/attitudes in cheerfulness-evoking situations. Seriousness facets include prevalence of serious states, perceiving everyday happenings as important, planning tendency, preferring activities with concrete rational reasons, sober communication, and a humorless attitude (SE1–SE6). Use the facet model when detailed assessment or hypothesis testing about subcomponents is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item construction criteria (rational-theoretical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Items for the long form were chosen to satisfy multiple content and quality criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items should be (1) short and understandable, (2) of diverse content, (3) covering the construct-related behavior and attitudes comprehensively, (4) be free of extreme levels of social desirability, (5) suitable for adolescents and adults, (6) not biased toward particular populations, and (7) logically related to the target constructs but not overlapping with similar but irrelevant constructs (original wording from Ruch et al., 1996).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid content-saturated items / humor-preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Questionnaires should be largely free of items that reference specific humor materials, formats, or culturally-specific content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid content-saturated items (references to certain comedians, jokes, or formats) because these lower generalizability and introduce bias across age/cultural groups; aim for content-general expressions of tendencies and attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item wording polarity and negations
rubrics_metrics.description: Because cheerfulness, seriousness, and bad mood are antithetical, item polarity must be handled carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most items should be positively poled; negatively poled items can inadvertently index another trait (e.g., 'I don't feel like laughing' might indicate sadness). Use negations only when they represent standing expressions used in everyday language and after careful consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response format
rubrics_metrics.description: The STCI utilizes a four-point answering format for both trait and state versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response anchors used: 1 = strongly disagree to 4 = strongly agree. Maintain consistent four-point format for comparability across versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-form item-reduction criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria used to derive the 60-item standard trait form from the 106-item long form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider (a) the best corrected item-to-total correlation (CITC), (b) item content and representation of items of all facets, (c) roughly equal representation of the facets (with core facets getting more weight if equal representation not possible), and (d) avoidance of very similar items regarding content or linguistic usage (Ruch et al., p.316).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrected item-to-total correlation (CITC) threshold and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Use CITC values to evaluate individual item discrimination and as a criterion for selection/exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A minimal CITC > 0.30 is used as a practical threshold; report mean CITC per facet/scale. Items with low CITC (< ~0.30) are candidates for revision or removal. The paper reports mean facet CITCs and notes how many items did not reach > 0.30.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal consistency reliability (Cronbach's alpha)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report and aim for high internal consistency for trait total scores and acceptable-to-high alphas for facets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper reports trait total alphas in the high range (e.g., CH α ≈ 0.89–0.93; SE α ≈ 0.87–0.91; BM α ≈ 0.93–0.94). Facet alphas can be lower (some facets ~0.51–0.88); consider revising facets with low alpha. Use alpha alongside CITC when judging scale quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test–retest stability expectations (traits vs states)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect high retest stability for trait measures and lower stability for state measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported one-month retest stability for traits was high (between ~0.77 and 0.86). State measures should show low test–retest correlations in line with their expected temporal variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorial validity and model testing (CFA/EFA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use confirmatory factor analysis to test the hypothesized facet → trait → three-factor structure and compare alternative factor models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test multiple alternative models (e.g., one-factor, two-factor combinations, three-factor with correlated facets, three-factor with cross-loadings) and evaluate fit. Confirm that homologous facets load on their intended trait and that the three-factor (cheerfulness, seriousness, bad mood) structure fits the data better than competing structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multitrait–multimethod (MTMM) approach for convergent/discriminant validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use MTMM and CFA to separate trait, method, and error variance and to demonstrate convergent and discriminant validity across self- and peer-reports and aggregated states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convergent validity: homologous scales (same trait across methods) should correlate highly; discriminant validity: correlations among different traits should be lower. Aggregated state measures should correlate more strongly with traits than single-state measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive validity with external/behavioral criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish predictive validity by relating trait/state scores to behavioral, physiological, or experimental outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: trait cheerfulness predicts frequency/intensity of laughter, responsiveness to humor stimuli, pain tolerance after humor induction, neural activation patterns, and coping humor. Provide concrete external criteria and show expected directional relations (e.g., cheerfulness positively related to humor responses; bad mood negatively related).

rubrics_metrics.name: State-version design and sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: State version items should capture current feelings and be sensitive to mood alternations and manipulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design state items to measure mood-quality facets (e.g., cheerful mood vs hilarity; soberness/pensiveness/earnestness; melancholy/ill-humor). The state form was iteratively reduced to 10 items per scale and should show satisfactory internal consistency (reported α ~0.85–0.94) and sensitivity to experimental and natural mood variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language adaptation and translation procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: A multi-step, expert-driven translation/adaptation procedure to ensure conceptual equivalence and item sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps used: (1) independent translations by two experts, (2) comparison and discussion to form a coordinated list, (3) review by two additional native researchers for orthographic/grammatical corrections checked for content correspondence, (4) further discussion with additional experts including the original scale author to produce a pilot version. Use experts familiar with the construct and measurement challenges (e.g., negations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple versions and target groups (scope of application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide different STCI versions for different uses: long trait form for facets, standard short trait form for economical assessment, state forms, child/adapted versions, self- and peer-report forms, workplace forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select version according to purpose: STCI-T <106> for facet-level analyses; STCI-T <60> for economical trait assessment (total scores only); shorter STCI-T <30> or state versions (STCI-S <30>, <20>, <18>) for brief screening or specific contexts. Adapt items linguistically/age-appropriately for children and different report sources (peer, parent, teacher).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling and generalizability considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for samples that permit generalization across age, gender, cultural groups, and methods (self vs peer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes sample characteristics (e.g., university samples, gender imbalance) and recommends future studies to obtain more balanced samples in terms of gender ratio and broader demographics. Also test measurement invariance across languages and nationalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and procedural standards for data collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure voluntary participation, informed consent by virtue of survey completion, anonymity, and compliance with institutional ethical guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure participants can refrain from participation at any time without consequences. Document ethics committee requirements or waivers and protect anonymity. For peer reports, provide clear instructions for returning data (e.g., mail) and confirm rater familiarity with the target (report time spent together, familiarity rating).
